# Datasets in detail {#sec-datasets-detail}

**Every dataset in the book reaches the model through one file format and
one set of conventions, so the differences between datasets are in the
physics and the boundary data, not in the plumbing.** This appendix is the
reference for those conventions and for each dataset's provenance, size,
conversion, field names, sign conventions, normalization and splits. The
protocol chapter (@sec-datasets) says what each dataset is and what the
model receives, at the depth a reader of the results needs. This appendix
is where to look when reproducing a lane, writing a converter for a new
dataset, or finding which cases a number was scored on.

*Before this chapter:* the input contract of @sec-using-inputs (boundary
cells with positions, outward normals and measure weights; $K$ global unit
vectors; $S$ global scalars; $n_b$ per-cell boundary scalars; interior
queries with their scalars) and the names of the tasks in @sec-datasets.

```{python}
#| label: setup-datasets-detail
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
PF = RES / "problem_figures_2026-09-22"
meta = {p.stem: json.load(open(p)) for p in sorted(PF.glob("*.json"))}
```

```{python}
#| label: setup-problem-figures
#| include: false
import json
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection

def load_problem(name):
    """One representative sample of a dataset, reduced for plotting (results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/)."""
    z = np.load(PF / f"{name}.npz"); m = json.load(open(PF / f"{name}.json"))
    return {k: z[k] for k in z.files}, m

def bc_segments(ax, pts, cells, kinds, lw=4.0, zorder=3):
    """Draw line cells colored by boundary-condition kind (keys of palette.BC)."""
    segs = pts[cells][:, :, :2]
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[BC[k] for k in kinds], linewidths=lw, capstyle="butt", zorder=zorder))

def field_scatter(ax, xy, v, s=3.0, signed=False, vmin=None, vmax=None):
    if signed:
        lim = max(abs(np.nanmin(v)), abs(np.nanmax(v))) if vmin is None else None
        norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=(-lim if vmin is None else vmin), vmax=(lim if vmax is None else vmax))
        return ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], c=v, s=s, lw=0, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm, rasterized=True)
    return ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], c=v, s=s, lw=0, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, rasterized=True)

def small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, label, **kw):
    cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.035, pad=0.02, **kw); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    cb.set_label(label, fontsize=8.5)
    return cb

def bc_legend(ax, kinds, loc="lower right", extra=()):
    from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
    handles = [Line2D([], [], color=BC[k], lw=4, label=BC_LABEL[k]) for k in kinds] + list(extra)
    ax.legend(handles=handles, loc=loc, fontsize=8, frameon=True, facecolor="white", edgecolor=BASELINE)
```

## Conventions shared by every dataset {#sec-data-conventions}

**A converted case is one native `DomainMesh` file (`.pdmsh`): an
`interior` point cloud, one or more named `boundaries`, and a
`global_data` dictionary.** The datasets differ in which of these the
model reads and in what the boundary cells carry.

- **Two reader layouts.** The *surface* datasets (DrivAerML Surface task,
  HiLiftAeroML, SHIFT-SUV, DeepJEB++) read only the boundary mesh: the
  reader walks into the boundary tensordict
  (`<case>.pdmsh/_tensordict/boundaries/<name>`), merges the parent
  file's `global_data` onto it (`MeshReaderWithGlobalData`), and the
  terminal transform `MeshToDomainMesh` places the prediction points at
  the cell centroids. The *interior* datasets (DrivAerML Volume task,
  AirfRANS, the solids and OLBC sets) read the whole file
  (`DomainMeshReader`): the interior points are the queries and the
  boundary is kept whole whenever the cell budget exceeds its size.
- **Signed distance is positive outside the solid.** Interior nodes of a
  solid carry `sdf` $\le 0$; fluid points outside a body carry `sdf` $> 0$.
  `sdf_normals` is the gradient of that field, so it is the outward normal
  at the boundary. Converters negate a source that stores the opposite sign
  (OLBC stores the distance positive inside and a gradient pointing into
  the domain).
- **Boundary conditions are per-cell scalars.** Each labeled region is a
  0/1 indicator on the boundary cells (`bc_fixed`, `bc_loaded`,
  `bc_dirichlet`, …) and each prescribed value is a scalar on the cells it
  applies to and zero elsewhere (`bc_pressure`, `bc_value_g`, `bc_disp_x`,
  …). Where a traction vector exists it is stored too (`traction`,
  `bc_load`), but ISLA has no per-cell vector input. The traction on a
  pressed face is $-p\,n$, recoverable from the pressure scalar and the
  cell normal the model already sees. GeoTransolver has no boundary-token
  path, so the same labels and values are also written as nodal fields on
  the interior points (`tag_*`, `bc_*_node`) and enter its local embedding
  there.
- **Global vectors are unit directions and must be data of the problem.**
  For external aerodynamics `ComputeFreestreamDirection` writes `U_inf_dir`
  from the solver's velocity; for a loaded solid the load direction is the
  global vector. Where the targets are components in a fixed frame (the
  stress components of Tensile2d and of the OLBC elasticity set), the
  stress is predicted as a symmetric tensor and the components are read
  off it (@sec-isla-heads). Feeding the dataset's axes $+x, +y$ as global
  vectors is rejected: they are not a datum of the PDE (@sec-pose-prior). A dataset with no global
  direction ($K = 0$) runs ISLA with the eager geometry kernel; the fused
  kernel is written for $K = 1$.
- **Normalization statistics come from the manifest.** Every converter
  writes `manifest.json` next to the files with the named split lists and
  a `_stats` block of per-field mean and standard deviation pooled over the
  training split; the dataset yaml copies those values into
  `NormalizeMeshFields` (targets, and standardized input fields) and
  `StandardizeDomainGlobalField` (global scalars). Vector targets use one
  isotropic standard deviation (the Frobenius value divided by
  $\sqrt{2}$ in two dimensions), so a component's scale is not rescaled
  per axis.
- **Splits are named lists in the manifest; nested rungs are prefixes of
  one permutation.** Where a dataset publishes splits they are used
  unchanged (HiLiftAeroML, AirfRANS, SHIFT-SUV, PLAID's official ladder,
  OLBC's train/test). Where it does not (GINOT lug), or where a validation
  set has to be carved out (Tensile2d), the draw is a fixed-seed
  permutation recorded in the manifest, and every smaller rung is a prefix
  of the larger one, so a rung differs from the next only by the cases it
  lacks.

| dataset | converter | dataset yaml | ISLA yaml |
|---|---|---|---|
| DrivAerML (Surface, Volume) | native files from the dataset release | recipe `datasets/drivaer_ml_surface.yaml`, `drivaer_ml_volume.yaml` | recipe `conf/model/isla_surface.yaml`, `isla_volume.yaml` |
| HiLiftAeroML | native files | recipe `datasets/highlift_surface.yaml` | recipe `conf/model/isla_surface.yaml` |
| SHIFT-SUV | native files | recipe `datasets/shift_suv_surface.yaml`, `shift_suv_estate_surface.yaml`, `shift_suv_fastback_surface.yaml` | as DrivAerML |
| AirfRANS | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/airfrans_convert.py` | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/airfrans_volume.yaml` | `results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/isla_volume_airfrans.yaml` |
| PLAID Tensile2d | `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/plaid_tensile2d_convert.py` | `…/datasets/plaid_tensile2d.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_tensile2d.yaml` |
| GINOT Bracket Lug | `…/datasets/ginot_lug_convert.py` | `…/datasets/ginot_lug_volume.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_lug.yaml` |
| OLBC Poisson, OLBC elasticity | `…/datasets/olbc_convert.py --set {poisson,elasticity}` | `…/datasets/olbc_poisson.yaml`, `olbc_elasticity.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_olbc_poisson.yaml`, `isla_olbc_elasticity.yaml` |
| DeepJEB++ | `…/datasets/deepjebpp_convert.py` | `…/datasets/deepjebpp_surface.yaml` | `…/datasets/isla_surface_deepjebpp.yaml` |

"Recipe" is the unified external-aerodynamics recipe root (`examples/cfd/external_aerodynamics/unified_external_aero_recipe`); `…/datasets/` abbreviates `results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/`. The GeoTransolver yamls sit beside the ISLA yamls with the prefix `geotransolver_`. {#tbl-data-files}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-data-samples
#| output: asis
rows = [
    ("DrivAerML", "drivaer", "surface cells", "n_surface_cells", "volume points", "n_interior_points"),
    ("HiLiftAeroML", "hilift", "surface cells", "n_surface_cells", None, None),
    ("SHIFT-SUV (fastback)", "shift_suv", "surface cells", "n_surface_cells", None, None),
    ("AirfRANS", "airfrans", "boundary segments", "n_boundary_cells", "interior points", "n_interior_points"),
    ("PLAID Tensile2d", "tensile2d", "boundary segments", "n_boundary_cells", "nodes", "n_nodes"),
    ("GINOT Bracket Lug", "lug", "boundary triangles", "n_boundary_cells", "nodes", "n_nodes"),
    ("OLBC Poisson", "olbc_poisson", "boundary segments", "n_boundary_cells", "nodes", "n_nodes"),
    ("OLBC elasticity", "olbc_elasticity", "boundary segments", "n_boundary_cells", "nodes", "n_nodes"),
]
out = "| dataset | sample case (split) | boundary | interior |\n|---|---|---:|---:|\n"
for name, key, blab, bkey, ilab, ikey in rows:
    m = meta[key]
    split = m.get("split", m.get("family", ""))

print(": Size of the one case drawn in each problem figure of @sec-datasets, read from the figure metadata. How to read this: one case per dataset, not a mean; the aerodynamic surfaces are sampled to 200,000 cells per step under the reporting protocol, the solids and OLBC sets are read whole. Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/*.json. {#tbl-data-samples}")
```

## DrivAerML {#sec-data-drivaer}

**484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants in one far-field
condition; the boundary is the vehicle surface alone, and the two tasks
read different parts of the same files.** Each case is a `run_<id>`
directory holding a `domain_*.pdmsh` with the vehicle boundary
(`boundaries.vehicle`, triangles), the tetrahedral volume mesh with its
point fields, the watertight `*_single_solid.stl.pmsh` of the body, and
`global_data` with the far-field conditions `U_inf` (38.89 m/s along $x$),
`rho_inf`, `p_inf` (zero: the pressure is gauge), `nu` and `L_ref` (5 m).
The reader divides coordinates by `L_ref`, so a car spans about one unit.
The sample car in @tbl-data-samples has 17.0 million surface cells and
160 million volume points; @sec-interior states the volume range across
cars as 150 to 166 million.

- **Surface task.** The recipe reads the boundary tensordict directly
  (`run_*/*.pdmsh/_tensordict/boundaries/vehicle`). Fields
  `pMeanTrim` and `wallShearStressMeanTrim` (time-averaged) are
  nondimensionalized from the case's own `global_data`
  (`NonDimensionalizeByMetadata`: pressure by the far-field dynamic
  pressure, stress likewise) and renamed `pressure` and `wss`; `wss` is
  further scaled by a fixed standard deviation (0.00313). Normals are
  recomputed from the faces after centering (`ComputeSurfaceNormals`);
  the cell subsample and `DropDegenerateCells` follow; `MeshToDomainMesh`
  puts the prediction points at the cell centroids. `U_inf_dir` is written
  from `U_inf` before centering so the augmentation block (axis-aligned
  rotations about $z$, used by the baselines' pose lanes only) rotates it
  with the geometry.
- **Volume task.** `DomainMeshReader` on `run_*/domain_*.pdmsh` with the
  interior as a point cloud (tetrahedral topology dropped), the vehicle
  boundary subsampled by cells, and the STL as an extra boundary from
  which `ComputeSDFFromBoundary` writes `sdf` and `sdf_normals` at the
  query points (pseudo-normal sign, exact on the watertight STL) before
  the STL is dropped. `UMeanTrim`, `pMeanTrim`, `nutMeanTrim` become
  `velocity` (by $|U_\infty|$), `pressure` (by the dynamic pressure) and
  `nut` (standardized with mean 4.8e-4 and standard deviation 9.4e-4,
  m²/s).
- **What is not an input.** The ground plane and the wind-tunnel
  boundaries are present in the source files and are read by no
  configuration in the book; every model sees the vehicle surface only.
- **Splits.** One validation set of 48 cars, fixed across every
  experiment and shared by the two tasks; 435 training cars, with nested
  rungs of 27, 54, 109 and 218 for the data-efficiency ladder
  (@sec-data-efficiency); one variant is in neither set. The
  sampling-density and pose probes evaluate the same 48 cars with
  transformed inputs (@sec-discretization-centerpiece).
- **License.** The dataset is distributed by its authors under their own
  terms; this program's artifacts do not restate them.

## HiLiftAeroML {#sec-data-hilift}

**1,800 compressible RANS cases on a full grid of 180 high-lift wing
geometries by ten angles of attack, in imperial units, with curated
manifests for every split the book uses.** The geometries vary the flap
and slat settings by Latin hypercube; the angles run from 4° to 22° in
steps of 2°, so the far-field direction $\hat g_1$ varies per case and
carries the angle. Each case is a `geo_LHC<nnn>_AoA_<a>` directory; the
recipe reads the boundary tensordict
(`geo_LHC*/*.pdmsh/_tensordict/boundaries/vehicle`) and merges the
parent's `global_data` (`U_inf`, `p_inf`, `rho_inf`, `T_inf`, `L_ref`).
Units are slug, inch, second and Rankine: the far-field speed is 2,679.5
in/s, and the problem figure converts positions to meters for display
only. The targets are the projected averages `PROJ(AVG(P))`,
`PROJ(AVG(T))`, `PROJ(AVG(RHO))`, `PROJ(AVG(U))` and `AVG(TAU_WALL)` on
the surface cells, nondimensionalized from the case's `global_data`
(`NonDimensionalizeByMetadata`), renamed `pressure`, `temperature`,
`density`, `velocity`, `tau_wall`, and then standardized with fixed
constants in the dataset yaml (pressure mean −0.5 and standard deviation
1; temperature 1.00 / 0.002; density 1.0 / 0.02; velocity 0.20; wall
shear 0.003). The sample case in @tbl-data-samples has
291 million surface cells, the largest surface in the book, so a
200,000-cell draw is a $10^{-3}$ sample of it.

- **No interior task.** The dataset's volume files carry interior
  coordinates for 31 of the 1,800 cases and no interior fields, so
  HiLiftAeroML has no boundary-to-interior task on this cluster
  on this cluster; AirfRANS is the second interior dataset for that
  reason.
- **Dataset revision.** Every split in the book is a curated manifest of
  revision `bbec30bcfc6103309c1375c5228b3ad0a586bfaf`, in which six cases'
  force coefficients are surface-field integrations rather than solver
  monitor means; the book's force errors never use the dataset's
  coefficients as reference.
- **License.** As for DrivAerML, not restated here.

### Splits {#sec-data-hilift-splits}

**Each HiLiftAeroML split holds out one question, and the splits are the
dataset's curated manifests, used unchanged.** @tbl-hilift-splits and
@fig-hilift-splits, in @sec-splits, list them. Provenance is the dataset
revision named above.

The other datasets' splits are stated in their own sections: DrivAerML's
48-car validation set and nested training rungs (@sec-data-drivaer),
AirfRANS's published `full`, `reynolds` and `aoa` manifests
(@sec-data-airfrans), SHIFT-SUV's two families (@sec-data-shift-suv), and
the fixed-seed permutations of the solids and OLBC sets
(@sec-data-tensile2d, @sec-data-lug, @sec-data-olbc).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="The HiLiftAeroML manifests overlap, so a test split is sealed per checkpoint, not per program"}
The manifests are separate but not disjoint. The angle-of-attack and stall
test sets between them contain every one of the 180 geometries. The
360-case data-efficiency test set shares 179 cases with them, the geometry
test set 182 and the deflection test set 182 (37 and 40 of their cases also
sit in the shared validation set). A test split is therefore *held out per
checkpoint*, since no model evaluated on it trained on it. But once the
regime-extrapolation tests are read, no HiLiftAeroML geometry remains
unexposed at the level of the program, and no later evaluation on these
manifests is an independent program-level confirmation
(@sec-limits-validation).
:::

## AirfRANS {#sec-data-airfrans}

**1,001 two-dimensional incompressible RANS ($k$–$\omega$ SST) solutions
around NACA-family airfoils at Reynolds numbers of 2 to 6 million and
angles of attack of −5° to 15°, with published split manifests, converted
once from raw VTK.** The source (Bonnet et al., 2022) ships one directory
per case, `airFoil2D_SST_<speed>_<aoa>_<NACA parameters>`, with an
`_internal.vtu` volume slice of about 177,000 cells carrying velocity `U`,
pressure `p`, eddy viscosity `nut` and the signed distance
`implicit_distance` at the points, an `_aerofoil.vtp` polyline and a
`_freestream.vtp` of the far boundary. The chord is 1 m and the kinematic
viscosity 1.56e-5 m²/s.

- **Conversion** (`airfrans_convert.py`, @tbl-data-files). The interior is
  a point cloud in three dimensions at $z = 0$ with `velocity` (N, 3),
  `pressure`, `nut`, `sdf` (the file's `implicit_distance`, positive
  outside the airfoil) and `sdf_normals`, the in-plane unit vector from the
  nearest airfoil point to the query, computed in the converter because the
  recipe's SDF transform expects a triangulated surface. The boundary
  `airfoil` is line cells in three dimensions with precomputed in-plane
  outward normals (a curve in three dimensions has no cell normals of its
  own) and the segment lengths as `quadrature_measure`. `global_data`
  holds `U_inf` (parsed from the case name and checked against the
  freestream boundary's velocity), `U_inf_dir`, `U_inf_mag`, `aoa_deg`,
  `Re` and the NACA parameters.
- **Normalization** (`airfrans_volume.yaml`). Pressure is kinematic
  ($\rho_\infty = 1$, $p_\infty = 0$) and is divided by
  $\tfrac{1}{2} |U_\infty|^2$; velocity by $|U_\infty|$; `nut` keeps its
  units and is standardized (mean 7.9e-4, standard deviation 2.4e-3,
  m²/s, from the converter's per-case statistics).
- **What the model receives.** ISLA: the airfoil cells, `U_inf_dir` as
  the one global vector, `U_inf_mag` as the one global scalar, and the
  interior queries with `sdf` as the query scalar; outputs pressure and
  `nut` as scalars and velocity as a vector. On a planar problem the
  three-dimensional vector head's out-of-plane basis coefficient is
  learnable to zero. GeoTransolver-volume: the interior points with
  coordinates, `sdf` and `sdf_normals`, and the inlet velocity through the
  unit-direction rule (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
- **Splits** (the dataset's manifest, used unchanged). `full`: 800 train /
  200 test; `scarce`: 200 train; `reynolds`: 504 / 496, an extrapolation
  in Reynolds number; `aoa`: 804 / 196, an extrapolation in angle of
  attack. The training-case axis of the scaling study uses nested rungs of
  50, 100, 200 and 400 airfoils inside `full` (@sec-compute-allocation).
  Every case has about 179,000 interior points; the interior task queries
  100,000 of them per case per step (@sec-protocol).
- **License.** As for DrivAerML, not restated here.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-airfrans
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The AirfRANS problem, on one test airfoil. Top: the boundary the model
#|   sees, the airfoil polyline of about a thousand segments with their
#|   outward normals (every twelfth drawn), the inlet direction $\hat g_1$
#|   (black arrow, the one global vector, at the angle of attack) and the inlet
#|   speed as the one global scalar; the interior queries carry the signed
#|   distance to the airfoil. Middle: the pressure coefficient
#|   $C_p = p / \tfrac{1}{2} U_\infty^2$ (kinematic pressure) at the interior
#|   mesh points in a window around the airfoil. Bottom: the speed ratio
#|   $|U| / U_\infty$ at the same points. What varies per sample is the
#|   airfoil shape, the inlet speed and its direction. What the model
#|   predicts: pressure, velocity and turbulent viscosity at the queries. How
#|   to read this: the queried domain extends well beyond this window (its
#|   extent is printed); the dots are 70,000 of the case's 179,000 mesh points
#|   and their density follows the mesh, fine near the wall and in the wake.
#|   Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/airfrans.npz.
#| code-fold: true
A, Am = load_problem("airfrans")
bp, bc, bn = A["bnd_points"], A["bnd_cells"], A["bnd_normals"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
ip = A["int_points"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 7.2), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.22))
ax = axes[0]
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(bp[bc][:, :, :2], colors=BC["free"], linewidths=2.0, zorder=3))
k = slice(None, None, 12); ax.quiver(mid[k, 0], mid[k, 1], bn[k, 0], bn[k, 1], color=MUTED, scale=28, width=0.0025, headwidth=3, zorder=2)
u = A["U_inf_dir"]; ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.45 + 0.3 * u[0], 0.38 + 0.3 * u[1]), xytext=(-0.45, 0.38), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(-0.1, 0.40, f"inlet: uniform flow along $\\hat g_1$ at {Am['aoa_deg']:.2f}° (the global vector); $U_\\infty$ = {Am['U_inf_mag']:.1f} m/s (the global scalar); Re = {Am['Re']:.2g}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ib = A["interior_bbox"]
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 1.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.55); ax.set_ylabel("y / chord [–]")
ax.set_title(f"the boundary: {Am['n_boundary_cells']:,} line cells (position, normal, length), a no-slip wall; queries fill {ib[0,0]:.0f} < x < {ib[1,0]:.0f}, {ib[0,1]:.0f} < y < {ib[1,1]:.0f} chords", fontsize=9.2)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, ip[:, :2], A["int_cp"], s=2.5, signed=True, vmin=-1.0, vmax=1.0); map_axes(ax); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.55)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(bp[bc][:, :, :2], colors=INK, linewidths=0.8, zorder=3)); ax.set_ylabel("y / chord [–]")
ax.set_title("pressure coefficient $C_p$ at the interior points (target)", fontsize=9.5)
small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$C_p$ [–]", extend="both")
ax = axes[2]
sc = field_scatter(ax, ip[:, :2], A["int_umag"], s=2.5, vmin=0, vmax=1.3); map_axes(ax); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.55)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(bp[bc][:, :, :2], colors=WHITE, linewidths=0.8, zorder=3)); ax.set_ylabel("y / chord [–]"); ax.set_xlabel("x / chord [–]")
ax.set_title("speed ratio $|U| / U_\\infty$ at the interior points (target)", fontsize=9.5)
small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$|U| / U_\\infty$ [–]", extend="max")
plt.show()
```

## SHIFT-SUV {#sec-data-shift-suv}

**Sport-utility bodies in two rear-end families, estate and fastback,
read with DrivAerML's transform pipeline frozen so that a DrivAerML
checkpoint can be evaluated on them unchanged.** The curated manifest
separates the estate family (794 / 99 / 100 cases for training /
validation / test) from the fastback family (796 / 99 / 99); the frozen
inventory with the split hashes and the exclusion policy is
`results/shift_suv_full_dataset_inventory_2026-07-29/inventory.json`.
The recipe reads each run's `domain.pdmsh` boundary tensordict
(`run_*/domain.pdmsh/_tensordict/boundaries/vehicle`) under the family
subdirectory, and merges the case's `U_inf`, `p_inf`, `rho_inf`, `nu`,
`L_ref`. The sample fastback in @tbl-data-samples has 5.0 million surface
cells.

- **What is the same as DrivAerML.** `L_ref` is 5.0 m in both datasets,
  so the nondimensional coordinates are on the same scale; the same
  nondimensionalization, the same `wss` standard deviation and the same
  subsampling are applied; the fields `pressure_average` and
  `wall_shear_stress_average` are the time-averaged analogues of
  DrivAerML's `pMeanTrim` and `wallShearStressMeanTrim` (SI units verified
  against the release's `units.json`).
- **What differs, and how it is handled.** SHIFT-SUV stores absolute
  pressure with `p_inf` = 101,325 Pa where DrivAerML stores gauge pressure
  with `p_inf` = 0. The shared transform $(p - p_\infty) / q_\infty$ gives
  a proper pressure coefficient for both, with no correction. The
  far-field speed is 30.0 m/s against DrivAerML's 38.89, a Reynolds number
  about 1.3 times lower. Every model receives the unit direction only and
  none receives the Reynolds number, so this is a covariate shift
  identical for every architecture. It is reported alongside the
  geometry-family shift rather than corrected.
- **Role.** The fastback family is held out from every model in the book
  and is the zero-shot target of the cross-family transfer measurements
  (@sec-scoreboard-200k); the estate training split is a training source
  only where a two-family model is compared.
- **License.** As for DrivAerML, not restated here.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-shift-suv
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The SHIFT-SUV zero-shot target, on one fastback case. The vehicle surface
#|   (150,000 of its 5 million cells at their centroids) colored by the
#|   pressure coefficient $C_p = (p - p_\infty) / \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_\infty^2$,
#|   seen from the side and from above; the black arrow is the far-field
#|   direction $\hat g_1$. What varies per sample is the geometry; the far-field
#|   speed is fixed and lower than DrivAerML's, a covariate shift every model
#|   sees alike since none receives the Reynolds number. What the model
#|   receives is exactly what it receives on DrivAerML (positions, normals,
#|   areas, $\hat g_1$), which is what makes the zero-shot transfer possible.
#|   How to read this: the same color scale as @fig-problem-drivaer, so the
#|   two bodies can be compared by eye. Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/shift_suv.npz.
#| code-fold: true
S_, Sm = load_problem("shift_suv")
sp, cp = S_["surf_points"], S_["surf_cp"]
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=-1.5, vmax=1.0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.0, 1.15], hspace=0.15))
ax = axes[0]
depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 2]], sp[:, 1], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
U = S_["U_inf"]; bb = S_["surf_bbox"]; x0 = bb[0, 0] - 1.9; z0 = 0.5 * (bb[0, 2] + bb[1, 2])
ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 1.2, z0), xytext=(x0, z0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(x0 + 0.6, z0 - 0.1, f"far field: $U_\\infty$ = {np.linalg.norm(U):.0f} m/s\nalong $\\hat g_1$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.2, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlim(x0 - 0.2, bb[1, 0] + 0.3)
ax.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax.set_title(f"side view: $C_p$ on the {Sm['family']} family", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
sc = depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 1]], sp[:, 2], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("y [m]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [m]"); ax.set_title("top view: $C_p$", fontsize=9.5)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=axes, fraction=0.025, pad=0.01, extend="min"); cb.set_label("$C_p$ [–]"); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

## PLAID Tensile2d {#sec-data-tensile2d}

**702 two-dimensional quasi-static elasto-viscoplastic tension cases of a
notched specimen (Safran; CC-BY-SA-4.0; Hugging Face
`PLAID-datasets/Tensile2d`), of which the 500 official training samples
carry targets.** Plane strain, small deformations; each sample is an
unstructured triangle mesh of 6 to 12 thousand nodes with coordinates in
$[-1, 1]$ (a unit half-width), a pressure $P$ on the top edge that varies
per sample (negative $P$ pulls), a fixed bottom edge ($u_2 = 0$) with its
bottom-left node pinned ($u_1 = 0$), free curved notches, and five
constitutive scalars $p_1 \ldots p_5$ that vary too. The source is one
parquet column of pickled CGNS trees, read with pyarrow and numpy alone.
The 200 test samples and 2 out-of-distribution samples ship geometry and
input scalars but no output fields; the converter writes them under
`withheld/`, which the dataset pattern excludes.

- **Conversion** (`plaid_tensile2d_convert.py`). Interior: every node
  embedded at $z = 0$ with `displacement` (N, 3) = $(U_1, U_2, 0)$, `q`
  (cumulated plastic strain), `sig11`, `sig22`, `sig12` (MPa-scale, the
  dataset's units), `sdf` = −(distance to the outer boundary) and
  `sdf_normals`, plus the nodal tags `tag_top`, `tag_bottom`,
  `tag_bottomleft`. Boundary `outer`: every triangle edge owned by exactly
  one triangle, as line cells with outward in-plane normals, segment
  lengths as `quadrature_measure`, and the per-cell scalars `bc_loaded`
  (top edge), `bc_fixed` (bottom edge), `bc_pinned` (cells touching the
  pinned node), `bc_pressure` (= $P$ on loaded cells, so
  $\sigma_{22} = -P$ there) and `traction` (= $-P\,n$). `global_data`:
  `P`, `p1` … `p5`, `params` (6,), `has_targets`, and on training
  samples the output scalars `max_von_mises`, `max_q`, `max_U2_top`,
  `max_sig22_top` (never inputs).
- **What each model receives.** ISLA (`isla_tensile2d.yaml`): the outer
  cells with four boundary scalars (`bc_loaded`, `bc_fixed`, `bc_pinned`,
  `bc_pressure`), the six standardized input scalars `params_std` as
  global scalars, every node as an interacting query with `sdf`; outputs
  `q`, `sig11`, `sig22`, `sig12` as scalars and `displacement` as a
  vector. The configuration the book reports (`isla_tensile2d_tensor`)
  passes the load direction $+y$ as the one global vector and predicts the
  stress as a tensor. The earlier lanes that added the dataset's axes
  $+x, +y$ as two global vectors are the pose-prior diagnostic of
  @sec-pose-prior, not a configuration (the finding that scalar heads
  cannot produce components without a frame is @sec-isla-heads). GeoTransolver
  (`geotransolver_tensile2d.yaml`, 512 wide): the interior points with
  coordinates, `sdf`, `sdf_normals` and the three nodal tags in its local
  embedding, `params_std` as its global embedding, radii 0.05 / 0.2 / 0.8
  on the $[-1, 1]$ coordinates.
- **Normalization** (`plaid_tensile2d.yaml`, from the manifest `_stats`
  over `train_400`): `params` mean $[-45.0, 14.9, 450.8, 1502.6, 1496.5,
  75434.8]$ and standard deviation $[2.90, 2.87, 86.1, 286.1, 289.2,
  14613.8]$; `displacement` mean $[-3.38\times10^{-4}, 1.054\times10^{-3},
  0]$, isotropic standard deviation $8.22\times10^{-4}$; `sig11`
  $-0.127 / 28.4$; `sig22` $57.7 / 32.0$; `sig12`
  $8.1\times10^{-4} / 16.9$; `q` $1.73\times10^{-7} / 8.18\times10^{-6}$.
- **Splits.** The README's official nested ladder `train_8` …
  `train_500`, plus `val_100` (100 samples drawn with seed 0 from
  `train_500` minus `train_250`, so the official ladder up to
  `train_250` stays disjoint from it) and `train_400` (= `train_500`
  minus `val_100`). The book's ladder is 32 / 64 / 125 / 250 / 400 cases
  scored on `val_100`.
- **Pitfalls.** `q` is heavy-tailed under z-scoring (the per-case maximum
  ranges over four decades in `train_400`), so it is reported but excluded
  from the headline fields. With scalar heads and no tensor output ISLA
  fits the training set and validates 20 to 60 times worse than
  GeoTransolver: a component target is a view of a tensor, and the head
  must produce the tensor. The leaderboard's Tensile2d numbers are on the withheld test
  set and are not comparable to `val_100` figures.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-tensile2d
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The PLAID Tensile2d problem, on one validation specimen. Left: the outer
#|   boundary, 496 line cells, colored by the condition each carries: the top
#|   edge is loaded by the pressure $P$ (a traction $-P\,n$; negative $P$ pulls),
#|   the bottom edge is fixed ($u_2 = 0$) with its left corner pinned
#|   ($u_1 = 0$, marked), and the curved notches are free; the box lists the
#|   six global scalars of this sample and the arrow the load direction, the
#|   one global vector. Middle: the axial stress $\sigma_{22}$ at the
#|   mesh nodes. Right: the displacement magnitude $|u|$. How to read this:
#|   the specimen's coordinates and stresses are in the dataset's units (a
#|   unit half-width; MPa-scale stresses); the nodes drawn are all 6,171 of
#|   this sample and every one is a query token; the loaded and fixed edges
#|   are where the per-cell boundary scalars are nonzero. Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/tensile2d.npz.
#| code-fold: true
T, Tm = load_problem("tensile2d")
bp, bc = T["bnd_points"], T["bnd_cells"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
kinds = np.where(T["bc_loaded"] > 0.5, "flux", np.where(T["bc_fixed"] > 0.5, "value", "free"))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8, 4.2), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.15, width_ratios=[1.75, 1, 1]))
ax = axes[0]
ax.scatter(T["int_points"][:, 0], T["int_points"][:, 1], s=1.2, c=GRID, lw=0, rasterized=True)
bc_segments(ax, bp, bc, kinds, lw=4.5)
pin = mid[T["bc_pinned"] > 0.5]; ax.plot(pin[:, 0], pin[:, 1], marker="^", ms=9, color=BC["value"], mec=INK, ls="none", zorder=5)
ax.text(0.0, 1.07, f"top edge: pressure P = {Tm['globals']['P']:.1f} (flux)", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=BC["flux"], path_effects=halo())
ax.text(0.0, -1.08, "bottom edge: fixed $u_2$ = 0 (value)\ntriangle: pinned $u_1$ = 0", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=BC["value"], path_effects=halo())
ax.text(0.72, 0.0, "notches: free", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=BC["free"], rotation=90)
for v, lab in ((np.array([1, 0]), "$\\hat g_1$"), (np.array([0, 1]), "$\\hat g_2$")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(-2.4 + 0.35 * v[0], -1.1 + 0.35 * v[1]), xytext=(-2.4, -1.1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.6))
    ax.text(-2.4 + 0.5 * v[0], -1.1 + 0.5 * v[1], lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
g = Tm["globals"]
ax.text(-2.45, 1.0, "global scalars\n" + "\n".join(f"{k} = {g[k]:g}" for k in ("P", "p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5")), ha="left", va="top", fontsize=7.8, color=INK2,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc="white", ec=BASELINE))
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.55, 1.3); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.35); ax.set_ylabel("y [dataset units]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [dataset units]")
ax.set_title("conditions and global inputs", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, T["int_points"][:, :2], T["sig22"], s=4.0, vmin=0, vmax=float(np.quantile(T["sig22"], 0.995))); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [dataset units]")
ax.set_title("axial stress $\\sigma_{22}$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$\\sigma_{22}$ [MPa]", extend="max")
ax = axes[2]
um = np.linalg.norm(T["displacement"], axis=1)
sc = field_scatter(ax, T["int_points"][:, :2], um * 1e3, s=4.0, vmin=0); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [dataset units]")
ax.set_title("displacement magnitude $|u|$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$|u|$ [$10^{-3}$ length units]")
plt.show()
```

## GINOT Bracket Lug {#sec-data-lug}

**3,000 three-dimensional elastoplastic lugs (Liu, Koric et al.; Zenodo
15293036; CC BY 4.0), clamped at one end and pressed on the lower half of
the hole, with three geometry parameters and the pressure varying.** The
material is steel-like (E = 200 GPa, $\nu$ = 0.3, $\sigma_y$ = 380 MPa,
linear isotropic hardening H = 571.4 MPa). The raw release stores the
corner nodes of a quadratic hex mesh (5 to 15 thousand nodes, mean 9.5
thousand), the nodal von Mises stress in MPa, the surface node cloud, the
hex connectivity and `input_params` = [hole radius, length, thickness,
pressure] in m and Pa (pressures of 50 to 100 MPa). The lug lies along
$+x$: the flat end face at $x = x_{\min}$ is clamped, the far end is a
semicircular nose around the hole whose axis is parallel to $z$; the lug is
0.05 m wide.

- **Conversion** (`ginot_lug_convert.py`). Interior: every node with
  `von_mises` (MPa), `sdf` = −(distance to the surface), `sdf_normals`.
  Boundary `surface`: the boundary quads of the hex mesh (faces owned by one
  hex) split into triangles, outward normals, triangle areas as
  `quadrature_measure`, and the per-cell scalars `bc_fixed` (the clamped
  end face), `bc_hole` (the hole's cylindrical surface), `bc_loaded` (the
  lower half of the hole, $y$ below the axis), `bc_pressure` (MPa on loaded
  cells) and `traction` (= $-p\,n$, MPa). The fixed and pressed faces are
  identified geometrically from the paper's description; their areas match
  the paper's to 0.1%. `global_data`: `hole_radius`, `length`,
  `thickness` (m), `pressure` (Pa), `pressure_mpa`, `params` (4,),
  `sample_id`.
- **What each model receives.** ISLA (`isla_lug.yaml`): the surface
  triangles with four boundary scalars (`bc_fixed`, `bc_hole`,
  `bc_loaded`, `bc_pressure`), the four standardized design parameters as
  global scalars ($K = 0$, eager kernel), every node as a query with
  `sdf`; output `von_mises`. Coordinates stay in meters; the RMS-distance
  length unit absorbs the scale. GeoTransolver: the interior points with
  the nodal tags and the parameters as its global embedding.
- **Normalization** (manifest `_stats` over the 2,400 training lugs):
  `params` mean $[0.01249, 0.1001, 0.02251, 7.53\times10^{7}]$ and
  standard deviation $[1.44\times10^{-3}, 0.0116, 4.24\times10^{-3},
  1.44\times10^{7}]$; `von_mises` mean 150.2 MPa, standard deviation
  92.4 MPa over 22.8 million nodes.
- **Splits.** No indices are published (the paper holds out 20%), so the
  converter draws one seed-0 permutation: 600 test, 2,400 train, with
  nested `train_n300` / `train_n600` / `train_n1200` inside train. The
  book's ladder is 300 / 600 / 1,200 / 2,400 scored on the 600 test lugs.
- **Published numbers** (from the program's scout notes,
  `results/book_audit_2026-09-22/datasets_scout.md`): Transolver 2.74%
  (0.32% with the load scalar as input), GNOT 3.58%, GINOT 0.40% relative
  error on the authors' split; comparable in kind, not in split, to the
  book's figures.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-lug
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The GINOT Bracket Lug problem, on one test bracket. Left: the surface
#|   triangles that are the model's boundary tokens, colored by condition: the
#|   end face is clamped (value), the lower half of the hole carries the
#|   pressure (flux), the rest of the hole and the outer surface are free;
#|   orthographic view from above and in front (azimuth −60°, elevation 30°).
#|   Right: the von Mises stress at the mesh nodes projected along the hole's
#|   axis, the top face nearest; the box lists the four global scalars. What
#|   varies per sample: the hole radius, the length, the thickness and the
#|   pressure. How to read this: every node is a query token and the stress
#|   is the one target; the projection shows the top face's nodes over the
#|   interior ones, so the stress concentration at the hole is read on the
#|   surface. Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/lug.npz.
#| code-fold: true
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d.art3d import Poly3DCollection
Lg, Lm = load_problem("lug")
bp, bc = Lg["bnd_points"] * 1e3, Lg["bnd_cells"]
kinds = np.where(Lg["bc_loaded"] > 0.5, "flux", np.where(Lg["bc_fixed"] > 0.5, "value", "free"))
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1, projection="3d"); ax.set_proj_type("ortho")
tri = bp[bc]
face = np.array([BC[k] if k != "free" else "#d9d8d0" for k in kinds])
coll = Poly3DCollection(tri, facecolors=face, edgecolors="none", linewidths=0.1); ax.add_collection3d(coll)
ext = bp.max(0) - bp.min(0); c0 = 0.5 * (bp.max(0) + bp.min(0)); R = 0.5 * ext.max()
ax.set_xlim(bp[:, 0].min(), bp[:, 0].max()); ax.set_ylim(bp[:, 1].min(), bp[:, 1].max()); ax.set_zlim(bp[:, 2].min(), bp[:, 2].max()); ax.set_box_aspect(tuple(ext / ext.max()), zoom=1.0)
ax.view_init(elev=30, azim=-60); ax.set_axis_off()
ax.text2D(0.02, 0.90, "clamped end face: $u$ = 0 (value)", transform=ax.transAxes, color=BC["value"], fontsize=8.5, path_effects=halo())
ax.text2D(0.98, 0.14, "lower half of the hole:\npressure p (flux)", transform=ax.transAxes, color=BC["flux"], fontsize=8.5, ha="right", path_effects=halo())
ax.text2D(0.5, 0.02, "outer surface and upper hole: free", transform=ax.transAxes, color=BC["free"], fontsize=8.5, ha="center")
ax.set_title("boundary tokens and their conditions", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2)
ip = Lg["int_points"] * 1e3
sc = depth_scatter(ax2, ip[:, [0, 1]], ip[:, 2], Lg["von_mises"], s=6, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=float(np.quantile(Lg["von_mises"], 0.995))); map_axes(ax2)
g = Lm["globals"]
ax2.set_xlabel("x [mm]"); ax2.set_ylabel("y [mm]"); ax2.set_title("von Mises stress at the nodes (target)", fontsize=9.5)
small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax2, "von Mises [MPa]", extend="max")
fig.text(0.5, 0.0, f"this sample's global scalars: hole radius {1e3 * g['hole_radius']:.1f} mm, length {1e3 * g['length']:.1f} mm, thickness {1e3 * g['thickness']:.1f} mm, pressure {g['pressure_mpa']:.1f} MPa",
         ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

## OLBC {#sec-data-olbc}

**Two of the eighteen OLBC sets (Mousavi, Mishra, De Lorenzis; Zenodo
collection 10.5281/zenodo.18377370; CC BY 4.0), each one fixed mesh whose
boundary is cut per sample into random segments carrying labeled
Dirichlet, Neumann or Robin conditions with random values: the pure
complement of the aerodynamic datasets, where the geometry varies and the
boundary data are fixed.** Each set is 8,448 training and 256 test
samples on an unstructured triangle mesh; the files store, per sample, the
node coordinates (identical across samples), the distance field (positive
inside, zero on the boundary) and its gradient (pointing into the domain),
the solution and, per component and condition type, the boundary node
indices with the value $g$ (Robin also $\alpha$ in $\alpha u + \partial u
/ \partial n = g$). No connectivity is stored. The converter reconstructs
the boundary loops from the boundary node set by two-nearest-neighbor
chaining, and makes sure that the loops close.

- **poisson-square-bc5** (record 18377514): $-\nabla^2 u = f$ on
  $[-1, 1]^2$, "Mixed+" configuration: four random boundary segments each
  carrying a non-homogeneous Dirichlet, Neumann or Robin condition whose
  $g$ (and $\alpha$) are random sinusoids, and a random sinusoidal source
  $f$ per sample; 16,598 nodes, 1,120 on the boundary; linear FEM.
- **elasticity-circlehollow-m1** (record 18377539): linear elasticity of
  steel ($\lambda$ = 115 GPa, $\mu$ = 76.9 GPa), plane problem on the unit
  disc with two holes, all fields dimensionless (stress per 100 MPa,
  length per meter, so a displacement of $10^{-4}$ is 0.1 mm); per
  component and per sample the exterior circle is cut into four random
  segments: one free, one prescribed displacement (about $10^{-4}$) and
  two tractions (about $10^{-1}$); the smallest hole is clamped, the other
  is free; 11,786 nodes, 1,312 on the boundary over three loops;
  quadratic FEM stored at the vertices.
- **Conversion** (`olbc_convert.py --set {poisson,elasticity}`).
  Interior: every node at $z = 0$ with `sdf` = −(file distance), so nodes
  are $\le 0$ inside in the program's convention, `sdf_normals` =
  unit(−(file gradient)), outward at the boundary; Poisson: `u`,
  `source`, nodal labels `tag_dirichlet` / `tag_neumann` / `tag_robin`
  and values `bc_value_node`, `bc_robin_alpha_node`; elasticity:
  `displacement` (N, 3), `sig11` / `sig22` / `sig12`, `eps11` / `eps22` /
  `eps12` (stored, not targets), per-component tags and nodal values
  `bc_disp_node_*`, `bc_trac_node_*`. Boundary `outer`: line cells over
  all loops with normals outward from the solid (into a hole on hole
  loops; sign fixed by the file's gradient), segment lengths, `loop_id`
  (0 the exterior, then holes by decreasing node count), and per-cell
  labels and values: a cell takes the type shared by its two end nodes,
  the cell on either side of a segment junction takes its labeled end's
  type, and values are the mean of the labeled ends' $g$. Poisson:
  `bc_dirichlet`, `bc_neumann`, `bc_robin`, `bc_value_g`,
  `bc_robin_alpha` (0 off Robin cells); elasticity: `bc_dirichlet_x`,
  `bc_neumann_x`, `bc_disp_x`, `bc_trac_x` and the same for $y$.
  `global_data` holds only `sample_id`: the material is fixed and the
  source is a field.
- **What each model receives.** ISLA on Poisson
  (`isla_olbc_poisson.yaml`): the 1,120 cells with five boundary scalars
  (three one-hot types, $g$, $\alpha$), no global vector or scalar
  ($K = 0$, eager kernel), every node as a query with two query scalars,
  `sdf` and the standardized `source`; output `u`. ISLA on elasticity
  (`isla_olbc_elasticity_tensor.yaml`): the 1,312 cells with eight boundary
  scalars (per component: two one-hot types) and the prescribed
  displacement and traction stacked into two rank-1 boundary inputs
  (`StackScalarFields`), no global vector ($K = 0$), every node as a
  query with `sdf`; outputs the stress as a symmetric rank-2 tensor and
  `displacement` as a vector (`isla_olbc_elasticity_tensor.yaml`). The
  earlier scalar-input lanes with the domain axes as two global vectors
  are the pose-prior diagnostic of @sec-pose-prior. GeoTransolver-512
  on both: the interior points with coordinates, `sdf`, `sdf_normals` and
  the nodal tags and values in its local embedding; no global embedding
  (it works in absolute coordinates and needs no frame).
- **Normalization** (manifest `_stats` over train). Poisson: `u` mean
  $3.26\times10^{-3}$, standard deviation 1.0845; `source` mean
  $-7.0\times10^{-3}$, standard deviation 11.517 (standardized in place
  as an input). Elasticity: the boundary inputs `bc_disp_x` / `bc_disp_y`
  standard deviations $1.053\times10^{-4}$ / $1.047\times10^{-4}$ and
  `bc_trac_x` / `bc_trac_y` $6.05\times10^{-2}$ / $6.07\times10^{-2}$
  (means zero, so off-condition cells stay exactly zero); targets
  `displacement` isotropic standard deviation $3.18\times10^{-4}$,
  `sig11` $-1.57\times10^{-3} / 0.3127$, `sig22`
  $1.19\times10^{-3} / 0.3116$, `sig12` $4.9\times10^{-4} / 0.1825$.
  The displacement and traction values differ by three orders of
  magnitude, which is why they are separate fields rather than one
  `bc_value_g`.
- **Splits.** `train` (8,448) and `test` (256) as released, with nested
  `train_n512` / `train_n2048` as seed-0 prefixes of one permutation of
  train. The 512- and 2,048-case rungs train 500 epochs; the full rung
  trains 120 epochs, the same number of optimizer steps as the 2,048-case
  rung at 500, a stated deviation from the 500-epoch protocol
  (@sec-protocol).
- **Pitfalls and scope.** The Robin type appears in some Poisson samples
  and not others. One mesh per set: nothing measured here speaks to
  geometry generalization or discretization invariance; those axes remain
  with the aerodynamic and solids datasets.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-olbc-poisson
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The OLBC Poisson problem, $-\nabla^2 u = f$ on the square, on one test
#|   sample. Left: the boundary, 1,120 line cells, colored by the type of
#|   condition each segment carries in this sample (Dirichlet $u = g$, Neumann
#|   $\partial u / \partial n = g$, Robin $\alpha u + \partial u / \partial n = g$),
#|   with the prescribed value $g$ drawn as a curve offset from the edge (its
#|   scale in the corner). Middle: the source $f$, an input field given at the
#|   mesh nodes. Right: the solution $u$, the target. What varies per sample:
#|   where the segments are cut, which type each carries, the functions $g$
#|   and the source $f$; the mesh is the same for every sample. What the model
#|   receives: the boundary cells with positions, normals, lengths, a one-hot
#|   type and $g$ (and $\alpha$) as per-cell boundary scalars, no global
#|   vector, and every node as a query carrying $f$. How to read this: the
#|   Robin type appears in some samples and not others; this sample has none.
#|   Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/olbc_poisson.npz.
#| code-fold: true
O, Om = load_problem("olbc_poisson")
bp, bc, bn = O["bnd_points"], O["bnd_cells"], O["bnd_normals"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
kinds = np.where(O["bc_dirichlet"] > 0.5, "value", np.where(O["bc_neumann"] > 0.5, "flux", np.where(O["bc_robin"] > 0.5, "robin", "free")))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8, 3.7), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.3))
ax = axes[0]
bc_segments(ax, bp, bc, kinds, lw=4.0)
gscale = 0.12 / max(1e-9, float(np.abs(O["bc_value_g"]).max()))
off = mid[:, :2] + bn[:, :2] * (0.06 + gscale * O["bc_value_g"][:, None])
for k in ("value", "flux", "robin"):
    m = kinds == k
    if m.any():
        ax.scatter(off[m, 0], off[m, 1], s=2.5, c=BC[k], lw=0, rasterized=True)
ax.plot([1.08, 1.08], [-1.0, -1.0 + 0.12], color=INK2, lw=1.0); ax.text(1.12, -0.94, f"g = {float(np.abs(O['bc_value_g']).max()):.1f}", fontsize=7.5, color=INK2, va="center")
present = [k for k in ("value", "flux", "robin") if (kinds == k).any()]
bc_legend(ax, present, loc="lower center")
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-1.4, 1.4); ax.set_ylim(-2.05, 1.3); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("y [–]")
ax.set_title("conditions: type, and value $g$", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, O["int_points"][:, :2], O["source"], s=2.5, signed=True); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("source $f$ (input at the nodes)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$f$ [–]")
ax = axes[2]
sc = field_scatter(ax, O["int_points"][:, :2], O["u"], s=2.5, signed=True); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("solution $u$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$u$ [–]")
for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05); ax.set_yticklabels([])
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-olbc-elasticity
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The OLBC elasticity problem, plane-strain steel on a disc with two holes,
#|   on one test sample. Left: the three boundary loops; on the outer circle
#|   each of the two displacement components has its own condition, drawn as
#|   two concentric rings (outer ring: the $x$ component; inner ring: the $y$
#|   component), a prescribed displacement (value), a traction (flux) or free;
#|   the smaller hole is clamped in both components, the larger is free. The
#|   arrows are the dataset's coordinate axes, drawn for orientation only
#|   (they are not model inputs). Middle: the von
#|   Mises stress from the three stress components at the nodes. Right: the
#|   displacement magnitude. What varies per sample: where the outer circle is
#|   cut, which condition each segment and component carries, and the values.
#|   What the model receives: the loops' cells with normals, lengths, the
#|   per-component one-hot type and the prescribed displacement and traction
#|   components as rank-1 boundary inputs, and every node as a query; it
#|   predicts the stress tensor and the displacement. How to read
#|   this: all quantities are in the dataset's dimensionless units (stress per
#|   100 MPa, length per metre). Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/olbc_elasticity.npz.
#| code-fold: true
E, Em = load_problem("olbc_elasticity")
bp, bc, bn = E["bnd_points"], E["bnd_cells"], E["bnd_normals"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
def kinds_of(comp):
    return np.where(E[f"bc_dirichlet_{comp}"] > 0.5, "value", np.where(E[f"bc_neumann_{comp}"] > 0.5, "flux", "free"))
kx, ky = kinds_of("x"), kinds_of("y")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8, 3.9), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.3))
ax = axes[0]
outer = E["loop_id"] < 0.5
segs = bp[bc][:, :, :2]
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[outer] + 0.045 * bn[outer, None, :2], colors=[BC[k] for k in kx[outer]], linewidths=4.0, capstyle="butt"))
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[outer] - 0.0 * bn[outer, None, :2], colors=[BC[k] for k in ky[outer]], linewidths=4.0, capstyle="butt"))
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[~outer], colors=[BC[k] for k in kx[~outer]], linewidths=4.0, capstyle="butt"))
ax.scatter(E["int_points"][:, 0], E["int_points"][:, 1], s=0.8, c=GRID, lw=0, rasterized=True, zorder=0)
for v, lab in ((np.array([1, 0]), "$\\hat g_1$"), (np.array([0, 1]), "$\\hat g_2$")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(1.05 + 0.3 * v[0], 0.8 + 0.3 * v[1]), xytext=(1.05, 0.8), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.6))
    ax.text(1.05 + 0.46 * v[0], 0.8 + 0.46 * v[1], lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
bc_legend(ax, ["value", "flux", "free"], loc="lower center")
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-1.55, 1.6); ax.set_ylim(-2.15, 1.3); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("y [–]")
ax.set_title("conditions, per component\nouter ring: on $u_x$; inner ring: on $u_y$", fontsize=9.0)
vm = np.sqrt(E["sig11"] ** 2 - E["sig11"] * E["sig22"] + E["sig22"] ** 2 + 3 * E["sig12"] ** 2)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, E["int_points"][:, :2], vm, s=2.5, vmin=0, vmax=float(np.quantile(vm, 0.995))); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("von Mises stress (from targets)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$\\sigma_\\mathrm{vM}$ [–]", extend="max")
ax = axes[2]
um = np.linalg.norm(E["displacement"], axis=1)
sc = field_scatter(ax, E["int_points"][:, :2], um * 1e4, s=2.5, vmin=0); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("displacement $|u|$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$|u|$ [$10^{-4}$]")
for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05); ax.set_yticklabels([])
plt.show()
```

## DeepJEB++ {#sec-data-deepjeb}

**15,360 TRELLIS-generated jet-engine brackets in the SimJEB design space
(Yoo et al., KAIST; Hugging Face `KAIST-SmartDesignLab/DeepJEB-PP`; ODC-By
1.0), each under four static linear-elastic load cases (Ti-6Al-4V):
vertical, horizontal and diagonal forces and a torsion about $z$, with the
bolt holes clamped and the load shared over the lug bore.** The surface is
decimated to 25,000 vertices with per-vertex displacement (mm) and von
Mises stress (MPa) per load case, and explicit clamped-bolt and loaded-lug
vertex index sets.

- **Conversion** (`deepjebpp_convert.py`, @tbl-data-files). One file per
  (bracket, load): the FEM surface triangles re-wound outward, areas,
  `bc_fixed` / `bc_loaded` indicators, the traction `bc_load` (force cases
  $F\,d / A_{\text{loaded}}$; torsion the rigid-twist traction about the
  lug axis) with its two rotation-invariant scalars `bc_load_n` =
  $n \cdot t$ and `bc_load_mag` = $|t|$, cell-mean targets, and
  `global_data` with `load_dir` (the force direction or the moment axis),
  `load_type` one-hot [force, torque], the magnitude and the bracket's
  mass and volume.
- **What each model receives.** It is a surface task in the DrivAerML
  layout (`deepjebpp_surface.yaml`), with coordinates scaled from mm to
  0.1 m so a bracket spans about one unit. ISLA
  (`isla_surface_deepjebpp.yaml`) takes `load_dir` as the one global
  vector ($K = 1$, the fused kernel), the load-type one-hot as two global
  scalars (a moment axis is a pseudovector, so the model must know when
  the vector is an axis) and the four boundary scalars, and predicts von
  Mises stress and displacement at the cells.
- **Splits.** Grouped by SimJEB seed pair, because the brackets of one
  pair are a smooth family and must not straddle a split: a seed-0 draw of
  10% of the pairs is the test set, the rest train, with nested 256 /
  1,024 / 4,096-bracket rungs and per-load sub-splits; the authors'
  pair-grouped and random splits are kept under `official_*`. The ladder
  of @sec-surface-deepjeb is scored on 1,385 held-out brackets under all
  four loads (5,540 files).
- **Pitfalls.** A census of the labels found unphysical stress maxima on
  a tenth of the brackets; the clean split used in @sec-surface-deepjeb
  removes them. Published stress errors for Transolver, GNOT and GI-FNO
  are 30 to 37%, comparable in kind but not in split to the book's
  figures.

Every dataset in this appendix enters the book's evidence only with
GeoTransolver trained on it under the fair-comparison protocol
(@sec-fair-comparison) and a per-dataset preregistration before its first
lane. Datasets scouted but not adopted, and conversions under way, are in
@sec-program-status.
